title: Buy less, buy better: a decision framework for conscious consumption
subtitle: Questions to ask before a purchase to reduce spending, waste, and regret
excerpt: Most household waste is created at the point of purchase, buying more than is needed, buying lower quality that fails early, or buying items that serve one function when a multi-purpose alternative exists. A short decision framework applied before any non-consumable purchase reduces waste at the source rather than managing it later.
sourceNotes: Annie Leonard, The Story of Stuff (2010). Yvon Chouinard, Let My People Go Surfing (2005) on product longevity. Liz Marie blog practical minimalism framework.

content.text: The most sustainable product is one never manufactured. The second most sustainable is one bought once and used for decades. Neither of these outcomes requires sacrifice, they require applying a short decision sequence before purchase that identifies whether the thing is needed, whether the one you are buying will last, and whether you have already have something that does the job.

Do I already own something that does this? A different knife, a differently sized container, a tool that could be adapted. Before buying a new item, look at what you have. Most kitchens contain twelve items that perform the function of three.

Can I borrow it, hire it, or use a shared tool? A library of things, a tool-sharing community, or a neighbour. For items used less than five times in a decade, ownership is an inefficient way to access the function.

Can I buy it secondhand? Most household goods, clothing, tools, and furniture are available secondhand at 20 to 60% of new cost. For items where condition matters (electronics, tools with wear parts), inspect carefully. For items where condition matters less (books, ceramics, cast-iron cookware), secondhand is often superior.

If buying new, what is the expected life? Apply the cost-per-use principle: a cheap item used twice before failing costs far more per use than a quality item used hundreds of times. For items in regular continuous use, the higher-quality purchase is almost always the economic and environmental choice. For items used rarely, cheap is correct.

Can it be repaired when it fails? Choose products with replaceable parts and available service. A premium tool brand with a lifetime guarantee and a spare-parts programme is worth more than a no-name item whose manufacturer has ceased trading.

For any non-emergency purchase, wait 30 days before buying. This eliminates impulse purchases driven by novelty. Keep a list of things you considered buying and revisit it monthly. Items that still appear necessary after 30 days are still wanted; items that no longer appear on the list were passing preferences that evaporated on their own.
